textTitles: Oakhill Allotments — rules for plot holders

Returns and refunds: guidance for shop staff

paragraphs.text: Harbour Ferry — winter timetable, 1 November to 31 March. Boats leave the town pier at twenty minutes past every hour from 7.20 am to 6.20 pm, and return from the island at ten to the hour. There is no 1.20 pm sailing on weekdays, when the crew take their break. The crossing takes eighteen minutes in normal conditions and is cancelled only in a strong easterly wind, which usually gives at least two hours’ warning on the company website.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: A single adult fare is £4.60 and a return £8.20. Children under five travel free; those aged five to fifteen pay half. A book of ten single tickets costs £38 and may be shared between members of a household. Bicycles are carried free of charge, but there is space for only six on each boat and they are taken in the order passengers arrive. Dogs travel free on a lead and must stay on the open deck.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Tickets are bought at the pier office, which opens fifteen minutes before the first sailing, or from the crew on board if the office is closed. The office does not take cards for amounts under £3. Passengers with pushchairs and wheelchairs board first and use the ramp at the front of the boat; the ramp is not available at the island pier at low tide, and at those times the crew will carry luggage but cannot carry passengers.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Oakhill Allotments — rules for plot holders

paragraphs.text: Oakhill Allotments — rules for plot holders, agreed at the annual meeting. Plots are let for one year from 1 October and the rent is £42, payable within a month of the renewal notice. Half plots are available to new members and cost £24. A member who does not cultivate at least two thirds of the plot by the end of June will receive a written warning, and the plot may be let to someone else if nothing has changed eight weeks later.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Water is available from the standpipes between April and September only; hoses may not be left running unattended, and sprinklers are not permitted at any time. Bonfires are allowed on Saturdays after 4 pm between October and February, and never at other times of the year. Sheds must be no larger than two metres by three and may not be used for sleeping. Hens are permitted on full plots with the committee’s written agreement; cockerels and bees are not.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The main gate is locked at dusk, and every member receives one key, which may not be copied. Children are welcome but must be supervised, and the site is not insured for bicycles left inside the gates. Tools kept in the communal shed are borrowed by writing your name in the book by the door and returned the same day. The waiting list is held by the secretary and moves roughly ten places a year, so new applicants should expect to wait.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: C
texts.title: Community transport: what a volunteer driver does

paragraphs.text: Community transport: what a volunteer driver does. Our drivers take people to hospital appointments, to the shops and to day centres when no bus runs at the right time. You use your own car, and the scheme pays 45 pence a mile from the moment you leave home until you return; the payment is not taxed as income because it covers costs rather than time. Journeys are offered by text the week before, and you accept only the ones that suit you. Nobody is ever asked to explain a refusal.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Before your first journey there are four steps. You complete an application with two referees; we carry out a criminal record check, which takes about three weeks; you show your licence, insurance certificate and an MOT that has at least six months to run; and you attend a half-day session on assisting passengers, which covers wheelchairs, walking frames and what to do if a passenger becomes unwell. Your own insurer must be told that you carry passengers for a voluntary scheme; almost all treat this as ordinary use and do not increase the premium.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: On the day, arrive five minutes early and telephone the office if the passenger does not answer the door, rather than leaving. You may help a passenger to the car and carry shopping to the doorstep, but you should not enter the house, lift a passenger, or handle their money; where shopping has to be paid for, the office arranges it in advance. If a passenger asks you to make an extra stop, this is usually fine for a short errand, but the office should be told so that the next booking is not missed.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Drivers tell us the work is enjoyable and occasionally heavy. The same passengers are often booked to the same driver, which people like, though it means that when someone dies you will hear about it. Support is available: the coordinator calls every driver once a month, and there is a group that meets in the library on the first Tuesday. If you want to stop, for a while or for good, say so — we would rather keep you on the list for later than lose you altogether.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: D
texts.title: Returns and refunds: guidance for shop staff

paragraphs.text: Returns and refunds: guidance for shop staff. A customer who returns an unused item with a receipt within twenty-eight days is entitled to a refund to the original payment method. Without a receipt, offer an exchange or a credit note at the current selling price, and check the item against our own labels: we do not accept goods that were not bought here, however similar they look. Sale items may be returned on the same terms unless the ticket says otherwise.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Faulty goods are different and the twenty-eight days do not apply. Within six months of purchase the law assumes the fault was there when the item was sold, so do not ask the customer to prove it; offer a repair, a replacement or a refund, and let the customer choose between the first two. After six months, send the item to the workshop for an opinion before deciding. Never tell a customer that a fault is their responsibility because the packaging has been thrown away.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Online orders returned to the shop follow the online rules, which are more generous: fourteen days from delivery to change your mind for any reason, and no reason need be given. Process these through the returns screen, not the till, so that the warehouse is credited. Items marked "made to order" cannot be returned unless faulty, and this is printed on the order confirmation; if a customer says they did not see it, take their details and pass the case to the duty manager rather than refusing at the counter.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Two rules apply to everything above. Refunds are made to the card that paid, never in cash, unless the purchase itself was in cash. And if you are unsure, say that you will check rather than guessing: a wrong refusal costs us a customer and a wrong refund costs us the item, but a five-minute wait costs nothing. The duty manager can authorise an exception to any of this, and the reason is written in the returns book so that the next person sees it.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century the covered market was treated as a problem. Town councils across Europe and North America looked at their market halls — draughty nineteenth-century buildings full of small traders selling meat, cloth and vegetables — and saw dirt, low rents and a use of valuable land that no longer paid. Many were demolished outright; others were left to decay until the roof failed and demolition became the obvious answer. The supermarket, arriving with parking and predictable prices, seemed to have settled the argument.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The argument has reopened, and not for sentimental reasons. A town centre with empty shops has a measurable problem: footfall falls, the remaining shops lose trade, rents fall further and the cycle continues. Councils looking for something that brings people into the centre on a weekday have noticed that the markets which survived do exactly that, and that they do it with very little floor space per trader. A hall with forty stalls can hold as many businesses as a street of shops, and each of them starts with a rent measured in tens rather than thousands.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: That last point is the one traders talk about. A stall in a restored hall typically costs a fraction of a shop lease, is taken by the week rather than by the year, and carries no obligation to repair the building. For someone testing an idea, this is the difference between starting and not starting. A study of one restored market found that a third of its traders had moved on within three years, which sounds like failure until you ask where they went: rather more than half of those who left had taken a shop of their own nearby.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Restoration is not cheap, and the money rarely comes from the market itself. Roofs, drainage and electrical systems in a building of that age consume most of a budget before anything visible is done, and the halls that reopened in the past decade were almost all paid for by a mixture of public grants and heritage funds. Councils justify the spending by what happens around the hall rather than inside it, and the evidence for that is real but slow: shop occupancy within a few streets tends to improve over five to ten years, not in the first season.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The most common mistake is to restore the building and forget the trade. A hall filled entirely with coffee, cake and craft stalls looks lively on an opening weekend and struggles by the second winter, because nobody does a weekly shop there. The markets that hold up combine the two: enough food, fish, fruit and household goods to give people a reason to come every week, and enough prepared food and small workshops to give them a reason to stay. Managers who have done both say the ratio matters more than the design of the stalls.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Hours have had to change as well. A market that opened at six in the morning and shut at two in the afternoon served a town where one adult in a household stayed at home; the same hours now exclude most of the people the market needs. Late opening one evening a week, and Sunday trading where it is allowed, consistently increase takings, but they also increase the working day of traders who are usually self-employed and were already working long hours. Several halls have solved this by staffing the evening with a shared team rather than asking each stall to stay open.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Not every restoration works, and the failures are informative. Halls that reopened with rents set to recover the cost of the works emptied within two years; halls whose management was contracted out to a company paid per stall let filled up with whatever would pay, which usually meant the same phone-case and sweet stalls found in every shopping centre. The halls that have done best are run by a manager with a brief that mentions the mix of trades, and with the freedom to refuse a tenant who would pay.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: None of this makes the covered market a solution to the decline of town centres; it is too small for that. What it offers is a particular thing that is otherwise hard to buy: a place where a new business can open for the cost of a week’s rent, in a building the town already owns, with customers who are already walking past. That the same buildings were being demolished as worthless within living memory is worth remembering the next time something ordinary is described as finished.
paragraphs.label: H
